added_lemmas.statement:
Suppose \(h_n\le 1/32\), with \(a_\star=7/10\) and \(b=3/4\).  Then \(J_n\ge2\), the cutoff locations in \(\mathcal W_n\) lie in \([1/4,3/4]\), and the supports of distinct compliance profiles are disjoint up to Lebesgue-null endpoints.  The common potential-outcome table satisfies
\[
 q_{00}(x)=q_{11}(x)=\frac18,
 \qquad
 \frac1{40}\le q_{01}(x),q_{10}(x)\le\frac{29}{40},
 \qquad
 \sum_{u_0,u_1\in\{0,1\}}q_{u_0,u_1}(x)=1.
\]
All twelve latent masses defining every \(P_{j,\ell}\in\mathcal W_n\) are nonnegative and sum to one; the always-taker and never-taker masses are strictly positive everywhere, and the complier masses are strictly positive wherever \(w_{j,\ell}>0\).  No H\"older restriction on these latent cells is used.  The observable one-sided extensions are
\[
 \mu_{D,P_{j,\ell}}^{-}(x)=\frac{1-w_{j,\ell}(x)}2,
 \qquad
 \mu_{D,P_{j,\ell}}^{+}(x)=\frac{1+w_{j,\ell}(x)}2,
\]
\[
 \mu_{Y,P_{j,\ell}}^{-}(x)=\frac12-\frac{g_\star(x)w_{j,\ell}(x)}2,
 \qquad
 \mu_{Y,P_{j,\ell}}^{+}(x)=\frac12+\frac{g_\star(x)w_{j,\ell}(x)}2.
\]
They belong to the radius-\(M\), order-\(s\) H\"older ball.  The potential reduced forms are continuous at \(c_{j,\ell}\), and
\[
 d_{P_{j,\ell}}=\kappa_n,
 \qquad
 \theta_{P_{j,+}}=a_\star=\frac7{10},
 \qquad
 \theta_{P_{j,-}}=-a_\star=-\frac7{10}.
\]
Writing \(p_{j,\ell}^{D,Y}\) and \(p_{j,\ell}^{D}\) for the conditional observable cell probabilities, one has
\[
 p_{j,\ell}^{D,Y}(x,d,y)
 =p_{j,\ell}^{D}(x,d)m_{d,y}(x)
 \ge\frac{21}{320}>v.
\]
On either observable side,
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_{P_{j,\ell}}(Y\mid X=x)
 =\frac{1-g_\star(x)^2}{4}
  +g_\star(x)^2\operatorname{Var}_{P_{j,\ell}}(D\mid X=x)
 \ge\frac{51}{400}>v,
\]
and, when the treatment variance is positive,
\[
 \left|\operatorname{corr}_{P_{j,\ell}}(Y,D\mid X=x)\right|
 \le\frac7{\sqrt{51}}<\frac{63}{64}\le1-v.
\]
When the treatment variance is zero, the covariance is zero and the model-class convention applies.  Consequently \(\mathcal W_n\subset\mathcal P_n\).  Moreover, with \(R_\star\) as the outcome-invariant reference,
\[
 \frac{dP_{j,\ell}}{dR_\star}
 =1+(2D-1)\operatorname{sgn}(X-c_{j,\ell})w_{j,\ell}(X)
 \quad R_\star\text{-almost surely},
\]
so every product likelihood ratio is measurable with respect to \(\sigma((X_i,D_i)_{i=1}^n)\).  Finally,
\[
 \int_{-1}^{1}\psi(u)^2\,du=\frac{256}{315},
 \qquad
 E_{R_\star}\!\left[
 \frac{dP_{j,\ell}}{dR_\star}
 \frac{dP_{k,r}}{dR_\star}
 \right]=1
\]
for distinct \((j,\ell)\ne(k,r)\), and, for
\(Q_{\ell,n}=J_n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J_n}P_{j,\ell}^{\otimes n}\),
\[
 \chi^2(Q_{\ell,n},R_\star^{\otimes n})
 =\frac{\left(1+\frac{256}{315}\kappa_n^2h_n\right)^n-1}{J_n}.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Write \(a=a_\star=7/10\) and \(b=3/4\).  We verify each requirement in the order used by the lower bound.

First, \(h_n\le1/32\) implies \((16h_n)^{-1}\ge2\), and hence
\[
 J_n=\left\lfloor(16h_n)^{-1}\right\rfloor\ge2.
 \tag{1}
\]
For \(1\le j\le J_n\), the location formulas in \(\mathrm{def:outcome\mbox{-}invariant\mbox{-}family}\) give
\[
 c_{j,+}-h_n=\frac14+2(j-1)h_n\ge\frac14,
 \qquad
 c_{j,+}+h_n=\frac14+2jh_n\le\frac38,
 \tag{2}
\]
and similarly
\[
 [c_{j,-}-h_n,c_{j,-}+h_n]\subset[5/8,3/4].
 \tag{3}
\]
The centers within either label are separated by \(2h_n\); hence distinct supports meet, at most, at endpoints.  Supports carrying different labels lie in the disjoint plateau intervals in (2)--(3).  Therefore
\[
 w_{j,\ell}(x)w_{k,r}(x)=0
 \quad\text{for Lebesgue-almost every }x
 \quad\text{whenever }(j,\ell)\ne(k,r).
 \tag{4}
\]

Next, \(B'(t)=-30t^2(1-t)^2\le0\), \(B(0)=1\), and \(B(1)=0\).  Thus the definition of \(g_\star\) gives \(|g_\star(x)|\le a\).  With the corrected value \(b=3/4\), the common table is
\[
 q_{00}=q_{11}=\frac18,
 \qquad
 q_{01}=\frac{3/4+g_\star}{2},
 \qquad
 q_{10}=\frac{3/4-g_\star}{2}.
 \tag{5}
\]
Consequently its entries sum to one and
\[
 \min_{u_0,u_1,x}q_{u_0,u_1}(x)
 =\frac{3/4-7/10}{2}=\frac1{40}>0,
 \qquad
 \max_{u_0,u_1,x}q_{u_0,u_1}(x)
 =\frac{3/4+7/10}{2}=\frac{29}{40}.
 \tag{6}
\]
Because \(0\le w_{j,\ell}\le\kappa_n\le1/8\), the latent masses
\[
 \pi_{C,u_0,u_1,P_{j,\ell}}=w_{j,\ell}q_{u_0,u_1},
 \qquad
 \pi_{A,u_0,u_1,P_{j,\ell}}
 =\pi_{N,u_0,u_1,P_{j,\ell}}
 =\frac{1-w_{j,\ell}}2q_{u_0,u_1}
 \tag{7}
\]
are nonnegative.  The latter two are at least
\[
 \frac{1-1/8}{2}\frac1{40}=\frac7{640}>0,
 \tag{8}
\]
and the complier mass is positive wherever \(w_{j,\ell}>0\).  Summing (7) over the four potential-outcome cells and three response types gives
\[
 \sum_{u_0,u_1}q_{u_0,u_1}
 \left(w_{j,\ell}+\frac{1-w_{j,\ell}}2+
                    \frac{1-w_{j,\ell}}2\right)=1.
 \tag{9}
\]
This proves validity of the latent law using positivity alone; no smoothness of an individual latent cell is asserted or needed.

We next check exactly the observable and potential reduced forms that define \(\mathcal P_n\).  The response-type weights in (7) imply
\[
 E[D(z)\mid X=x]=\frac{1-w_{j,\ell}(x)}2+z,w_{j,\ell}(x).
 \tag{10}
\]
The common table (5), which is the same for every response type, gives
\[
 E[Y(0)\mid X=x]=\frac{1-g_\star(x)}2,
 \qquad
 E[Y(1)\mid X=x]=\frac{1+g_\star(x)}2.
 \tag{11}
\]
Combining (10)--(11) yields
\[
 E[Y(D(z))\mid X=x]
 =\frac12+g_\star(x)\left(z-\frac12\right)w_{j,\ell}(x).
 \tag{12}
\]
Equations (10)--(12), consistency, and \(Z=\mathbf 1\{X\ge c_{j,\ell}\}\) give the four displayed observable extensions in the statement.

It remains to verify their H\"older radii without imposing any latent-cell H\"older condition.  On \((-1,1)\),
\[
 \psi'(u)=-4u(1-u^2),
 \qquad
 \psi''(u)=-4+12u^2.
 \tag{13}
\]
Both \(\psi\) and \(\psi'\) join continuously to zero at \(\{-1,1\}\).  Hence
\[
 \lVert\psi'\rVert_\infty\le2,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Lip}(\psi')\le8.
 \tag{14}
\]
When \(s=1\), using \(h_n=32\kappa_n/M\), scaling (14) gives
\[
 \operatorname{Lip}(w_{j,\ell})
 \le\frac{2\kappa_n}{h_n}=\frac{M}{16}.
 \tag{15}
\]
When \(1<s\le2\), put \(\beta=s-1\).  Since \(h_n^s=32\kappa_n/M\), \(h_n\le1\), and a Lipschitz function on an interval of diameter at most one has \(\beta\)-H\"older seminorm bounded by its Lipschitz constant,
\[
 \lVert w_{j,\ell}'\rVert_\infty
 \le\frac{2\kappa_n}{h_n}
 =\frac{M}{16}h_n^{s-1}\le\frac{M}{16},
 \qquad
 [w_{j,\ell}']_{s-1}
 \le\frac{8\kappa_n}{h_n^s}=\frac{M}{4}.
 \tag{16}
\]
By (2)--(3), \(g_\star=a\) on the support of every \(+\) profile and \(g_\star=-a\) on the support of every \(-\) profile.  Since each \(w_{j,\ell}\) vanishes off its support,
\[
 g_\star w_{j,+}=a w_{j,+},
 \qquad
 g_\star w_{j,-}=-a w_{j,-}
 \quad\text{on }[0,1].
 \tag{17}
\]
Thus (15) gives observable Lipschitz constants at most \(M/32\) for treatment and \(aM/32=7M/320\) for outcome.  Equations (16)--(17) give derivative suprema bounded by the same constants and derivative H\"older seminorms at most \(M/8\) and \(aM/8=7M/80\), respectively.  More explicitly, the treatment extensions have supremum norm at most \(9/16\), while the outcome extensions have supremum norm at most \(1/2+a\kappa_n/2\le87/160\).  Hence even under the convention that the radius bounds the sum of the displayed norm components,
\[
 \frac9{16}+\frac{M}{32}+\frac{M}{8}\le M,
 \qquad
 \frac{87}{160}+\frac{7M}{320}+\frac{7M}{80}\le M,
 \tag{18a}
\]
where both inequalities use \(M\ge2\); for \(s=1\), deleting the seminorm term only strengthens them.  Thus each extension lies in the radius-\(M\), order-\(s\) H\"older ball required by \(\mathrm{ass:observable\mbox{-}holder\mbox{-}extensions}\).  Equations (10) and (12) are continuous at \(c_{j,\ell}\), proving the potential-reduced-form continuity condition.

Since \(w_{j,\ell}(c_{j,\ell})=\kappa_n\), the observable treatment extensions give
\[
 d_{P_{j,\ell}}=\kappa_n.
 \tag{18}
\]
The outcome extensions and (17) give
\[
 y_{P_{j,+}}=a\kappa_n,
 \qquad
 y_{P_{j,-}}=-a\kappa_n.
 \tag{19}
\]
The denominator in (18) is positive by \(\kappa_n>0\), so division in the definition of \(\theta_P\) is legitimate, and (18)--(19) yield the two claimed effect labels.  The cutoff is interior by (2)--(3), \(X\) is uniform by construction, and the sample law is the independent product of the displayed one-unit law.

For nondegeneracy, the common table makes the conditional law of \(Y\) given \((D=d,X=x)\) Bernoulli with success probability
\[
 E[Y\mid D=d,X=x]=\frac12+g_\star(x)\left(d-\frac12\right).
 \tag{20}
\]
Thus every conditional outcome margin is at least \((1-a)/2=3/20\).  On either side of the cutoff, every conditional treatment cell has probability at least \((1-\kappa_n)/2\ge7/16\).  The factorization caused by the common table therefore gives
\[
 p_{j,\ell}^{D,Y}(x,d,y)
 =p_{j,\ell}^{D}(x,d)m_{d,y}(x)
 \ge\frac7{16}\frac3{20}=\frac{21}{320}>\frac1{64}>v.
 \tag{21}
\]
Conditional variance and covariance decomposition applied to (20) give
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=x)
 =\frac{1-g_\star(x)^2}{4}
  +g_\star(x)^2\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X=x),
 \tag{22}
\]
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D\mid X=x)
 =g_\star(x)\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X=x).
 \tag{23}
\]
Since \(|g_\star|\le a\), (22) is at least
\[
 \frac{1-a^2}{4}=\frac{51}{400}>\frac1{64}>v.
 \tag{24}
\]
If \(V_D=\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X=x)>0\), then \(V_D\le1/4\), and (22)--(23) imply
\[
 |\operatorname{corr}(Y,D\mid X=x)|
 =\frac{|g_\star|\sqrt{V_D}}
        {\sqrt{(1-g_\star^2)/4+g_\star^2V_D}}
 \le\frac{a}{\sqrt{1-a^2}}
 =\frac7{\sqrt{51}}.
 \tag{25}
\]
Both sides are positive, and squaring shows
\[
 \frac{49}{51}<\frac{3969}{4096}
 \quad\text{because}\quad
 49\cdot4096=200704<202419=51\cdot3969.
\]
Hence \(7/\sqrt{51}<63/64<1-v\), where the last inequality uses \(v<1/64\).  If \(V_D=0\), (23) gives zero covariance, exactly as required by the convention in \(\mathrm{ass:observable\mbox{-}correlation\mbox{-}separation}\).  Equations (2)--(25) verify every member property in \(\mathrm{def:model\mbox{-}class}\), and therefore
\[
 \mathcal W_n\subset\mathcal P_n.
 \tag{26}
\]

Finally, under \(R_\star\), \(D\) is conditionally fair given \(X\), while the conditional outcome margin (20) is the same as under every \(P_{j,\ell}\).  Cancelling that strictly positive margin in the full observable density ratio gives, outside the null event \(X=c_{j,\ell}\),
\[
 L_{j,\ell}:=\frac{dP_{j,\ell}}{dR_\star}
 =1+(2D-1)\operatorname{sgn}(X-c_{j,\ell})w_{j,\ell}(X).
 \tag{27}
\]
This proves the asserted outcome invariance and \(\sigma(X,D)\)-measurability.  Direct integration gives
\[
 \int_{-1}^{1}\psi(u)^2\,du
 =2\left(1-\frac43+\frac65-\frac47+\frac19\right)
 =\frac{256}{315}.
 \tag{28}
\]
Conditioning on \(X\) under \(R_\star\) in (27) and using
\(E_{R_\star}[2D-1\mid X]=0\) shows
\[
 E_{R_\star}[L_{j,\ell}L_{k,r}]
 =1+\int_0^1
   \operatorname{sgn}(x-c_{j,\ell})
   \operatorname{sgn}(x-c_{k,r})
   w_{j,\ell}(x)w_{k,r}(x)\,dx.
 \tag{29}
\]
For distinct indices, (4) makes (29) equal to one.  For equal indices, the change of variables \(u=(x-c_{j,\ell})/h_n\) and (28) give
\[
 E_{R_\star}[L_{j,\ell}^2]
 =1+\frac{256}{315}\kappa_n^2h_n.
 \tag{30}
\]
Independence raises (29)--(30) to the \(n\)-th power.  Expanding the square of the equally weighted mixture likelihood ratio, with \(J_n\) diagonal and \(J_n(J_n-1)\) off-diagonal terms, yields
\[
 \chi^2(Q_{\ell,n},R_\star^{\otimes n})
 =\frac{\left(1+\frac{256}{315}\kappa_n^2h_n\right)^n-1}{J_n},
\]
as claimed.
added_lemmas.justification: The high-separation witness verifies class membership, positivity, observable smoothness, nondegeneracy, outcome invariance, and the exact second moment while increasing the two causal labels to distance \(7/5\).
added_lemmas.gap: Madrid Padilla, Yu, Wang, and Rinaldo (2022) aggregate unrestricted multivariate change signals; they do not construct this latent monotone fuzzy-RD subexperiment with an outcome channel that cancels from the likelihood ratio.
added_lemmas.consumer: The replacement finite-sample theorem uses this legal causal family to obtain the \(7/5\) connected-length coefficient while preventing outcome-assisted cutoff localization.

added_lemmas.statement:
Put
\[
 C_\psi=\frac{256}{315},
 \qquad
 C_h=\left(\frac{32}{M}\right)^{1/s},
 \qquad
 \lambda_w=(sC_\psi C_h)^{-1}
 =\frac{315}{256s}\left(\frac{M}{32}\right)^{1/s}.
\]
If \(h_n\le1/32\), then the high-separation outcome-invariant witness gives the finite-sample bound
\[
 L_n(\kappa_n)
 \ge\frac75\left[
 1-2\alpha-
 \sqrt{\frac{\left(1+C_\psi\kappa_n^2h_n\right)^n-1}{J_n}}
 \right]_+.
\]
Along every admissible triangular sequence,
\[
 \frac1s\log(1/\kappa_n)-C_\psi C_hT_n\longrightarrow+\infty
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}L_n(\kappa_n)
 \ge\frac75(1-2\alpha).
\]
In particular,
\[
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}
 \frac{T_n}{\log(1/\kappa_n)}<\lambda_w
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}L_n(\kappa_n)
 \ge\frac75(1-2\alpha).
\]
For \(s=1\), \(\lambda_w=315M/8192\).  The sufficient regime contains sequences on which the known-cutoff minimax length shrinks to zero: for every \(0<\gamma<(2+1/s)^{-1}\), the eventual choice \(\kappa_n=\rho_n(\log n)^\gamma\) satisfies the first displayed limit and \(L_n^{\mathrm{known}}(\kappa_n)\to0\).  The constant \(\lambda_w\) is an explicit one-sided witness threshold; this theorem does not claim that it is the exact critical frontier.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Let \(I_n\) be an arbitrary measurable connected interval rule satisfying the uniform coverage condition in \(\mathrm{def:minimax\mbox{-}length}\).  By \(\mathrm{prop:outcome\mbox{-}invariant\mbox{-}witness\mbox{-}high\mbox{-}separation}\), each component of \(Q_{+,n}\) is in \(\mathcal P_n\) and has causal target \(a_\star=7/10\), while each component of \(Q_{-,n}\) is in \(\mathcal P_n\) and has target \(-a_\star=-7/10\).  Averaging the componentwise honesty inequalities therefore gives
\[
 Q_{+,n}\{a_\star\in I_n\}\ge1-\alpha,
 \qquad
 Q_{-,n}\{-a_\star\in I_n\}\ge1-\alpha.
 \tag{31}
\]
For probability measures \(Q\ll R\), Cauchy--Schwarz applied to the density ratio yields the elementary inequality
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(Q,R)
 =\frac12E_R\left|\frac{dQ}{dR}-1\right|
 \le\frac12\sqrt{E_R\left(\frac{dQ}{dR}-1\right)^2}
 =\frac12\sqrt{\chi^2(Q,R)}.
 \tag{32}
\]
The triangle inequality for total variation, (32), and the equal chi-square identities for the two labels give
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(Q_{+,n},Q_{-,n})
 \le\operatorname{TV}(Q_{+,n},R_\star^{\otimes n})
    +\operatorname{TV}(Q_{-,n},R_\star^{\otimes n})
 \le
 \sqrt{\frac{\left(1+C_\psi\kappa_n^2h_n\right)^n-1}{J_n}}.
 \tag{33}
\]
Transfer the second event in (31) from \(Q_{-,n}\) to \(Q_{+,n}\) using the definition of total variation, and intersect it with the first event in (31).  The union bound and (33) imply
\[
 Q_{+,n}\{-a_\star,a_\star\in I_n\}
 \ge1-2\alpha-
 \sqrt{\frac{\left(1+C_\psi\kappa_n^2h_n\right)^n-1}{J_n}}.
 \tag{34}
\]
A connected subset of \(\Theta=[-1,1]\) containing both labels has Lebesgue length at least \(2a_\star=7/5\).  Since \(Q_{+,n}\) is the uniform mixture of in-class product laws,
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}E_P[|I_n|]
 \ge E_{Q_{+,n}}[|I_n|]
 \ge\frac75\left[
 1-2\alpha-
 \sqrt{\frac{\left(1+C_\psi\kappa_n^2h_n\right)^n-1}{J_n}}
 \right]_+.
 \tag{35}
\]
Taking the infimum over all honest rules proves the finite-sample assertion.

We now evaluate (35).  From the definition of \(h_n\),
\[
 h_n=C_h\kappa_n^{1/s},
 \qquad
 n\kappa_n^2h_n=C_hT_n.
 \tag{36}
\]
Whenever \(h_n\le1/32\), the number \(x=(16h_n)^{-1}\) is at least two.  Since \(\lfloor x\rfloor\ge x/2\) for \(x\ge2\),
\[
 J_n\ge\frac1{32h_n}.
 \tag{37}
\]
Using \(1+x\le e^x\), (36)--(37) bound the chi-square term in (35) by
\[
 \frac{\left(1+C_\psi\kappa_n^2h_n\right)^n-1}{J_n}
 \le32h_n\exp\{C_\psi n\kappa_n^2h_n\}
 =32C_h\kappa_n^{1/s}
   \exp\{C_\psi C_hT_n\}.
 \tag{38}
\]
The logarithm of the final expression is
\[
 \log(32C_h)-\frac1s\log(1/\kappa_n)+C_\psi C_hT_n.
 \tag{39}
\]
If
\[
 \frac1s\log(1/\kappa_n)-C_\psi C_hT_n\longrightarrow+\infty,
 \tag{40}
\]
then (40) first implies \(\log(1/\kappa_n)\to\infty\), because \(T_n>0\).  Hence \(\kappa_n\to0\), so \(h_n\to0\) and (37)--(39) apply eventually.  Equation (39) tends to \(-\infty\); therefore the square-root term in (35) tends to zero.  This proves
\[
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}L_n(\kappa_n)
 \ge\frac75(1-2\alpha).
 \tag{41}
\]

For the ratio corollary, suppose
\[
 \limsup_n\frac{T_n}{\log(1/\kappa_n)}<\lambda_w.
 \tag{42}
\]
Condition (42) forces \(\kappa_n\to0\): otherwise, along a subsequence bounded away from zero, \(T_n=n\kappa_n^{2+1/s}\) diverges at least linearly while \(\log(1/\kappa_n)\) stays bounded, contradicting (42).  Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) so that eventually
\[
 \frac{T_n}{\log(1/\kappa_n)}\le\lambda_w-\varepsilon.
\]
Using \(C_\psi C_h\lambda_w=1/s\), we obtain
\[
 \frac1s\log(1/\kappa_n)-C_\psi C_hT_n
 \ge C_\psi C_h\varepsilon\log(1/\kappa_n)
 \longrightarrow+\infty.
 \tag{43}
\]
Thus (42) implies (40), and (41) proves the stated corollary.  Substitution of \(s=1\) into the definition of \(\lambda_w\) gives
\[
 \lambda_w=\frac{315}{256}\frac{M}{32}=\frac{315M}{8192}.
\]

Finally, fix \(0<\gamma<(2+1/s)^{-1}\) and, for all sufficiently large \(n\), set
\[
 \kappa_n=\rho_n(\log n)^\gamma
 =n^{-s/(2s+1)}(\log n)^\gamma.
 \tag{44}
\]
This sequence is positive and eventually at most \(1/8\).  Direct calculation gives
\[
 T_n=n\kappa_n^{2+1/s}
 =(log n)^{\gamma(2+1/s)}=o(\log n),
 \tag{45}
\]
whereas
\[
 \log(1/\kappa_n)
 =\frac{s}{2s+1}\log n-\gamma\log\log n
 \asymp\log n.
 \tag{46}
\]
Equations (45)--(46) imply (40).  Also
\[
 \frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n}=(\log n)^{-\gamma}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The upper inequality in \(\mathrm{thm:known\mbox{-}cutoff\mbox{-}benchmark}\) now yields \(L_n^{\mathrm{known}}(\kappa_n)\to0\), while (41) remains in force.  This establishes the oracle-shrinking comparison.  Since no converse or attaining construction is supplied at or above \(\lambda_w\), the proof makes only the asserted one-sided claim.
added_lemmas.justification: The theorem converts exact location-mixture second moments into a finite-sample connected-length bound with coefficient \(7/5\) and evaluates the explicit one-sided witness elbow \(\lambda_w\).
added_lemmas.gap: M{\"u}ller and Song (1997) and Tuvaandorj (2020) study shrinking-jump location problems, but neither derives fixed-level connected fuzzy-RD LATE-interval length under a jointly vanishing compliance denominator and unknown cutoff.
added_lemmas.consumer: An empirical analyst can compare \(T_n/\log(1/\kappa_n)\) with the computable witness threshold \(\lambda_w\) to certify a regime in which every honest connected LATE interval has nonvanishing expected length.

proposed_definition_changes.reason: The high-separation legal witness uses discordance mass \(b=3/4\).  With \(a_\star=7/10\), this corrected table keeps every potential-outcome cell positive while leaving the outcome-invariant likelihood cancellation unchanged.

proposed.condition: For every \(V\in\{D,Y\}\) and \(\ell\in\{-,+\}\), the one-sided regression \(\mu_{V,P}^{\ell}\) admits an extension to \([0,1]\) in the radius-\(M\) H\"older ball of order \(s\), with the derivative interpreted in the usual way when \(s>1\).

proposed.condition:
For each \(\ell\in\{-,+\}\) and every \(x\) on side \(\ell\) of \(c_P\),
\[
 |\operatorname{Cov}_P(Y,D\mid X=x,\ell)|
 \le(1-v)\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_P(Y\mid X=x,\ell)
                    \operatorname{Var}_P(D\mid X=x,\ell)}.
\]
If \(\operatorname{Var}_P(D\mid X=x,\ell)=0\), then the covariance is zero and the display is interpreted as \(0\le0\), without forming a correlation coefficient.

proposed.comparator_claim: Their published analysis supplies the known-cutoff bias-aware Anderson--Rubin template and separate smoothness restrictions on observable outcome and treatment regressions; the present class adapts that template but is not their parameter space.
Their unknown-cutoff analysis obtains oracle substitution under a fixed discontinuity in a sharp-design treatment-effect problem.
Their ordered-modulus construction optimizes fixed-level expected length on convex fixed-index regression classes.
Their shrinking-jump location analysis does not convert cutoff multiplicity into fixed-level connected LATE-interval length with a vanishing first stage.

The paper studies nonparametric location estimation with a shrinking discontinuity under smoothness restrictions, but it neither yields the connected-LATE witness elbow nor validates the frozen fuzzy-RD moving-window profile.
Their multiscale work supplies scan architecture and exponential change-point control for step-function signals.
Their Gaussian and multiplier-bootstrap theory supplies general stochastic maximal-control tools, but such control cannot repair the deterministic population-score misranking proved here.
Their aligned multivariate change-channel analysis does not impose the latent monotone fuzzy-RD causal restrictions or derive the outcome-invariant \(7/5\) connected-length witness.
Their Bayesian model propagates unknown-cutoff posterior uncertainty into fuzzy-RD effect estimation.
Their working paper treats fuzzy regression discontinuity and unknown-discontinuity estimation in separate extensions.

prose_updates.tldr: The paper studies fixed-\(\alpha\) expected length of connected honest intervals for fuzzy-RD LATE when both the compliance jump and its unknown cutoff become statistically weak.  An outcome-invariant high-separation mixture gives the finite-sample lower bound with coefficient \(7/5\) and a nonshrinking limit below the explicit witness threshold \(\lambda_w=315( M/32)^{1/s}/(256s)\).  This is a one-sided elbow, not the exact critical frontier.  At \(s=1\), a total four-fold rectangular scan--refine--invert rule attains the known-cutoff order when \(n\kappa_n^3\) dominates \(\log(e/\kappa_n)\).  For \(s>1\), the frozen affine moving-window profile is disproved as a uniform localizer, so the detectable-region bracket and the fixed-level critical-window law remain open.

project_justification.gap: Known-cutoff weak fuzzy-RD inference and fixed-jump unknown-cutoff localization do not characterize honest connected LATE-interval length when the first-stage denominator and its location weaken jointly.  Existing shrinking-jump location results do not yield the explicit causal witness elbow \(\lambda_w\), its \(7/5\) connected-length coefficient, or an exact critical-window law.  In the higher-smoothness problem, general stochastic maximal inequalities are also insufficient because the frozen moving-window profile can be misranked already at the population level under separate one-sided smoothness.
project_justification.niche: The joint experiment combines a nonconvex union over cutoff locations, a causal outcome--treatment ratio, separate one-sided observable smoothness that permits a derivative kink, and fixed-level connected-length loss.  The high-separation common-outcome construction makes the full likelihood depend only on \((X,D)\), so outcome-assisted localization cannot evade its explicit location entropy.  The higher-smoothness counterexample separately shows that a locally affine compliance trend can make a displaced profile split fit better than the true split.
project_justification.fill: On one unchanged observable-law class, the project proves an exact finite-sample location-mixture converse with coefficient \(7/5\), evaluates its one-sided threshold \(\lambda_w=(sC_\psi C_h)^{-1}\), and gives a total four-fold interval attaining known-cutoff order on the Lipschitz face.  For \(s>1\), it proves an exact projection counterexample to the frozen profile and retains the proposed detectable-region bracket as an OEQ requiring a genuinely different estimator/profile or a negative resolution.  The exact critical-window frontier is not claimed.

prose_updates.related_work: Noack and Rothe (2024) supply the known-cutoff bias-aware Anderson--Rubin template and separate smoothness restrictions on observable outcome and treatment regressions. Our binary-outcome, uniform-design, unknown-cutoff triangular class adapts that template but is not their published parameter space.  Porter and Yu (2015) obtain unknown-cutoff oracle substitution under a fixed discontinuity in a sharp-design treatment-effect problem.  Frick, Munk, and Sieling (2014) motivate multiscale scan architecture, while Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, and Kato (2014) provide general stochastic maximal-control tools; neither prevents the deterministic population-score misranking in the higher-smoothness counterexample.  M{\"u}ller and Song (1997) and Tuvaandorj (2020) concern shrinking-jump or nonparametric location experiments; neither converts translated-cutoff multiplicity into the proved \(7/5\) fixed-level connected LATE-length bound below \(\lambda_w\), and no equation-level proposition from Tuvaandorj is used here.  Armstrong and Koles{\'a}r (2018) supply an ordered-modulus and test-inversion template for convex fixed-index classes.  Madrid Padilla, Yu, Wang, and Rinaldo (2022) study aligned multivariate change channels without the monotone fuzzy-RD causal restrictions or the common-outcome likelihood cancellation used here.  Kowalska, van de Wiel, and van der Pas (2025 version) use a Bayesian unknown-cutoff fuzzy-RD model, and Arai, Otsu, and Seo (2026) discuss fuzzy and unknown-discontinuity extensions separately.  The proved frontier advance is the explicit one-sided location-mixture converse together with Lipschitz oracle attainment; a replacement higher-smoothness procedure and the exact critical-window connected-length law remain open.
prose_updates.interpretation: The ratio \(T_n/\log(1/\kappa_n)\) compares local jump information with the number of disjoint candidate cutoffs.  Below the explicit witness threshold \(\lambda_w=(sC_\psi C_h)^{-1}\), the two mixtures with causal labels \(\pm7/10\) merge in total variation, so honesty and connectedness force asymptotic expected length at least \(7(1-2\alpha)/5\), even along sequences for which known-cutoff intervals shrink.  This sufficient converse does not locate the exact critical transition.  At \(s=1\), strong signal permits the proved rectangular scan and oracle-order inversion.  For \(s>1\), the frozen affine profile fails at the population level, so a different criterion or a negative frontier theorem is necessary.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The lower construction evaluates only one side of the critical experiment.  At \(T_n/\log(1/\kappa_n)\to\lambda_w\), the first-order coordinate does not determine the witness mixture limit because the second-order centering \(C_\psi C_hT_n-s^{-1}\log(1/\kappa_n)\) remains; above \(\lambda_w\), this chi-square argument becomes uninformative.  The higher-smoothness profile branch remains a total measurable map but is not a valid uniform localizer on the stated class: a legal population score favors a displaced split, and maximal inequalities cannot repair that deterministic failure.  Neither limitation affects the finite-sample \(7/5\) lower bound or the proved Lipschitz-face upper theorem, but the exact critical law, a replacement higher-smoothness estimator, and a matching slope-kink lower pair remain open.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The Wald interpretation, known-cutoff benchmark, strengthened finite-sample location-mixture barrier, and Lipschitz-face oracle attainment retain their stated scope.  The explicit \(\lambda_w\) condition is a sufficient one-sided witness threshold and is not advertised as the exact signal-to-entropy boundary.  The \(7/5\) coefficient comes from a legal common-outcome witness with \(a_\star=7/10\) and \(b=3/4\); no latent-cell H{\"o}lder restriction is imposed or claimed.  For \(s>1\), the paper proves only that the frozen common-versus-piecewise moving-window profile fails its proposed uniform localization inequality on the unchanged class; it does not conclude that every estimator fails or that the candidate detectable-region bracket is false.  No cross-side derivative matching, adaptation guarantee, disconnected-set result, or matched critical-window constant is added.  Noack--Rothe-style refers only to the observable-regression and nondegeneracy template; equality with, or inclusion in, their published parameter space is not claimed.

statement_notes.justification: The explicit positivity, observable smoothness, variance, correlation, factorization, and second-moment calculations make outcome-assisted localization fail on a legal high-separation causal subexperiment.
statement_notes.gap: Aligned multivariate change-point analyses do not provide a monotone fuzzy-RD latent construction whose outcome margin cancels exactly while its two LATE labels are separated by \(7/5\).
statement_notes.consumer: The finite-sample lower theorem uses the family to transfer honesty between opposite effect labels without allowing the outcome channel to eliminate the location-entropy barrier.

statement_notes.justification: The bound gives an explicit finite-sample connected-length certificate and evaluates the largest one-sided signal-to-entropy threshold delivered by this exact witness calculation.
statement_notes.gap: Known-cutoff weak-instrument inference and shrinking-jump cutoff-location rates do not imply the \(7/5\) connected LATE-length bound or the explicit threshold \(\lambda_w\) under a jointly unknown and vanishing first stage.
statement_notes.consumer: Analysts can compute \(\lambda_w\) and identify sequences on which an administratively undocumented cutoff makes every honest connected LATE interval nonshrinking, despite a shrinking known-cutoff benchmark.
